start.speaker: corin
start.text: Corin sets the axe down and wipes his hands on a rag that makes them dirtier. 'You're going east. I can tell by the boots; nobody buys boots like that to go west.' He tries a smile. 'If you want someone to carry things or stand between you and a hound, I've a strong back. But I should tell you before you ask: people who travel with me tend to come to grief. It's a sort of gift.'

choices.text: 'I'm going to Emberhold to ask the Order to ride against the Regent. I need someone who knows the way.'
'I need a sword at my side. Yours will do.'
[Insight] 'You've been waiting nine years for someone to tell you you're allowed to stop.'
'Tam says you're an idiot.'
'Another time, maybe.'

east.speaker: corin
east.text: The colour goes out of his face. 'Emberhold.' He looks at the road for a long moment. 'They won't ride. Not for you, not for anyone, and certainly not with me standing next to you.' Then he picks up his sword belt anyway. 'But you'll not walk up that road alone. That much I can still do.'

sword.speaker: corin
sword.text: 'It's notched,' he says, apologetically, buckling it on. 'And so am I. But we both still cut.' He shoulders the biggest pack in the yard before you can stop him. 'By your leave, then.'

seen.speaker: corin
seen.text: Corin opens his mouth to answer and nothing comes out. He stands there with the rag in his hands, a very big man looking suddenly very young. 'That's,' he says, and stops, and tries again. 'I'll get my sword.' He walks away quickly, and you hear him blow his nose very loudly in the stable.

wall.speaker: corin
wall.text: He laughs gently, as if you had made a kind joke. 'Nothing so interesting, I'm afraid. I'm only a man who's good at woodpiles.' He picks the axe back up. 'But if you need me, I'll be here. I'm always here.'

tam.speaker: corin
tam.text: Corin stares at you, then bursts out laughing, a great helpless bark that sends the Last Lamp's hens running. 'Tamsin Reed. She's still alive, then, and still cross.' He wipes his eyes on his wrist. 'If Tam's still talking to me, I suppose I'd better be worth it. Wait while I find my sword.'

start.speaker: corin
start.text: Camp is quiet. Corin sits with his back to a stone, eyes closed, lips moving. When you come closer you hear it: names, one after another, low and steady. 'Abel Fenn. Maud Fenn. Little Pip Fenn.' He stops when he notices you and looks almost guilty. 'Sorry. I say them every night. Tarrow's. Someone should, and the someone ought to be me.'

choices.text: Sit down beside him. 'Teach me one.'
'Do you ever put your own name at the end of that list?'
'Goodnight, Corin. A friend can keep watch too.' Leave him to it.

teach.speaker: corin
teach.text: He looks at you for a long moment. 'Hanna Mill. She ran the bakery. She once chased me out of it with a rolling pin for stealing a bun, and then gave me two.' You say it back to him. Hanna Mill. Something in his face eases, a little, like a knot loosened by one turn. 'Nobody's ever said one with me before.'

choices.text: Take his burned hand and press your lips to the scar.
'Then I'll say them with you. Every night you like.'

own.speaker: corin
own.text: Corin goes very still. 'No,' he says at last. 'I'm not dead.' Then, honestly, because he does not seem able to be anything else: 'Some nights I think it would be tidier if I were.' He says it gently, like a man describing the weather.

choices.text: 'I'd mind. Very much.' Take his hand and don't let go.
'You did what you were told, by a man who meant you to. That isn't a crime.'

hand.speaker: corin
hand.text: Corin makes a sound you suspect he did not intend to make. His fingers, the ones that don't open properly, close very carefully round yours. 'I didn't,' he says, 'I wasn't expecting,' and then gives up on sentences altogether and simply leans his forehead against yours until the fire burns down.

together.speaker: corin
together.text: So you do. He says each name and you say it after him, all forty-one, and when it is done he is quiet for a long time. 'That's the first night in nine years I've not felt like the only one carrying them.' He shifts, so his shoulder is warm against yours. 'Thank you. I mean that more than I know how to say.'

mind.speaker: corin
mind.text: Corin looks down at your joined hands as if they belong to someone else's story. 'You'd mind,' he repeats, wondering. Then, very quietly: 'Then I'll try to be a man worth minding about.' He doesn't let go either.

crime.speaker: corin
crime.text: 'Maybe.' He doesn't believe it. You can see him wanting to. 'Ask me again when the bell's back in Tarrow. Maybe I'll know by then.'

declined.speaker: corin
declined.text: 'Goodnight,' Corin says, and smiles at you with a warmth that asks for nothing. 'I'm glad of the company, whatever kind it is.' The names start again behind you, steady as rain.

start.speaker: corin
start.text: Corin has washed. Not just his face; all of him, and his hair is still damp, and he is holding a single red ember lily as if it might go off. 'I'd like,' he says, and stops, and starts again. 'By your leave. I'd like to court you. Properly. The old way, with flowers and walks and, ah. Poetry.' He has gone red to the ears. 'I wrote some. It's very bad. I thought you should know what you're agreeing to.'

choices.text: 'Read it to me.'
Take the lily. 'Yes. Court me, Corin.'
'Corin, I care about you. But not like that. I'm sorry.'

poem.speaker: corin
poem.text: He unfolds a scrap of paper with enormous dignity. 'Your eyes are like the dawn on Greyford ford. You walk the way a good horse walks. I would follow you across the Ash Fields. This one doesn't rhyme. I couldn't find anything for Fields.' He folds it up again. 'There are eleven more verses. Several are about your boots.'

choices.text: Laugh until you cry, and then kiss him.
[Performance] Take the paper and read it back to him like the greatest love poem ever written.
'It's lovely, Corin. But I can't be what you want.'

yes.speaker: corin
yes.text: He stares at you. 'Yes?' And then, with dawning, enormous delight: 'Yes.' He kisses your knuckles, which is entirely the wrong amount of kissing for the moment and also somehow exactly right. 'I'll do it properly. You'll see. I'll be a menace with flowers.'

laughed.speaker: corin
laughed.text: You laugh so hard you have to hold on to him, and halfway through he starts laughing too, helplessly, the two of you in the ash with the lily crushed between you. When you kiss him it tastes of honey brittle and woodsmoke. 'I'll take that as a yes,' he says, dazed. 'Or a review. Either way.'

performed.speaker: corin
performed.text: By the second line he has stopped breathing. By the fourth, about the boots, he has his face in his hands. When you finish he looks at you over his fingers. 'Nobody's ever,' he says, and doesn't finish, and kisses you instead, which is a better ending than any of his verses.

declined.speaker: corin
declined.text: Corin nods slowly, and the lily droops a little in his hand. 'Of course. Thank you for telling me straight; that's a kindness too.' He tucks the poem away. 'I'll still carry the heavy pack. That doesn't change.' And, to his credit, it never does.

start.speaker: corin
start.text: Corin has not lain down. He kneels by the dying fire with his sword point-down in front of him, the way knights keep vigil the night before an oath. When you sit beside him he doesn't stop. 'I swore to the crown once,' he says softly. 'Hold where you are set. I've been trying to keep that oath for twelve years with nobody left to keep it to.' He turns his head and looks at you. 'I'd like to set myself somewhere new. Beside you. If you'll have me there.'

choices.text: 'Then hold here.' Put your hand over his on the hilt.

effects.message: Corin works the iron ring off his finger, the one with Ashdown stamped inside it, and puts it on yours. Then he lies down at last, his burned hand in yours, and sleeps without saying a single name.

choices.text: 'Ask me again when the war is over, Corin.'

later.speaker: corin
later.text: 'I'll ask,' he says, steady as stone. 'I'll still be here to.' He keeps his vigil until dawn, and when you wake he has made breakfast for everyone and burned all of it.

start.text: Wenna is waiting at the chapel door when you arrive, arms folded, soot-black to the elbow. She doesn't look at Corin. Corin doesn't look at her. Between the two of you, with a block and tackle and a great deal of swearing from Wenna, the bell goes up into the bell-cote, and the new rope hangs down into the chapel where forty-one names are chalked on the wall.

choices.text: 'Wenna. It's yours to ring.'
[Insight] Ask Wenna to look at the wall before she rings it. Really look.
'Ring it together. Both of you.'
'Wait. Brother Lark was promised this bell. Send for Lark first.'

lark.speaker: marches_lark
lark.text: It takes an hour, and a boy from Cinderfold sent running. Then Brother Lark comes down the Tarrow road in a borrowed coat, the thorns picked out of their sleeves, and stops in the chapel door with both hands over their mouth. 'I rang it till the rope burned,' they say to nobody. Wenna looks at them for a long moment and moves over on the step to make room.

choices.text: 'Wenna. It's yours to ring.'
'Ring it together. Both of you.'

the_wall.text: Wenna looks. Forty-one names in blocky chalk, each one gone over again and again where the damp has faded it, nine winters of going over. Her mother's name is there. So is her own, crossed out, and above it, in smaller letters, the words: found alive, thank God. She puts her hand flat over it and stands like that a long time.

wenna_rings.text: Wenna takes the rope in her black hands and pulls. The bell is cracked and green and it does not matter at all: it rings out over the ash, one note, then another, then the whole bright clamour of it, rolling out across the Marches for the first time in twelve years. Behind you, Corin makes a sound like something tearing.

together.text: Wenna looks at Corin for the first time. Then she holds out the end of the rope. He stares at it as if it might burn him worse than the tower did. She shakes it at him, impatient. He takes it. Together they pull, and the bell rings out over the ash, one note, then another, then the whole bright clamour of it, rolling out across the Marches for the first time in twelve years.

names.speaker: corin
names.text: When the last note fades, Corin reads the names off the wall. All forty-one, steady, the way he has said them every night. At the end Wenna says, roughly, 'Forty-two.' He looks at her. 'The boy at the horn-post,' she says. 'He died there too, didn't he? Somebody ought to say his name and let him go.'

choices.text: Say it for him: 'Sir Corin Ashdown.'
Put your hand on Corin's shoulder and let him say it.

after.speaker: corin
after.text: Corin stands with his burned hand on the bellrope for a long moment. Then he laughs, wet and astonished, and sits down on the chapel step as if his legs have just been cut. 'I thought it would feel like being let off,' he says. 'It feels like being let go.' Wenna snorts and walks home. On the way out she knocks his shoulder with her fist, not hard. It is, you think, the closest thing to a blessing either of them has.
